claim: Leading strand DNA synthesis requires functional coupling between replicative helicase and DNA polymerase (DNAP) enzymes.
source: Leading strand DNA synthesis requires functional coupling between replicative helicase and DNA polymerase (DNAP) enzymes, but the structural and mechanistic basis of coupling is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding in the field, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: The structural and mechanistic basis of coupling between helicase and DNAP is poorly understood.
source: Leading strand DNA synthesis requires functional coupling between replicative helicase and DNA polymerase (DNAP) enzymes, but the structural and mechanistic basis of coupling is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: This study defines the precise positions of T7 helicase and T7 DNAP at the replication fork junction with single-base resolution.
source: This study defines the precise positions of T7 helicase and T7 DNAP at the replication fork junction with single-base resolution to create a structural model that explains the mutual stimulation of activities.
evidence: The study uses 2-AP fluorescence experiments to determine enzyme positions, as described in the Results section.

claim: Helicase and polymerase both participate in DNA melting.
source: Our 2-aminopurine studies show that helicase and polymerase both participate in DNA melting, but each enzyme melts the junction base pair partially.
evidence: This is supported by 2-AP fluorescence data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Each enzyme melts the junction base pair partially.
source: Our 2-aminopurine studies show that helicase and polymerase both participate in DNA melting, but each enzyme melts the junction base pair partially.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the moderate increase in 2-AP fluorescence with isolated enzymes compared to combined enzymes.

claim: The junction base pair is melted cooperatively when the helicase is located one nucleotide ahead of the primer-end.
source: When combined, the junction base pair is melted cooperatively provided the helicase is located one nucleotide ahead of the primer-end.
evidence: This is shown by 2-AP fluorescence experiments with different gap sizes between primer-end and fork junction (Figure 5E-H).

claim: Helicase stimulates the polymerase by promoting dNTP binding (decreasing dNTP Km).
source: The synergistic shift in equilibrium of junction base pair melting by combined enzymes explains the cooperativity, wherein helicase stimulates the polymerase by promoting dNTP binding (decreasing dNTP Km), polymerase stimulates the helicase by increasing the unwinding rate-constant (kcat), consequently the combined enzymes unwind DNA with kinetic parameters resembling enzymes translocating on single-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic measurements showing dNTP Km decreases from ~120 μM (with SSB) to 5 μM in the presence of helicase (Figure 3G).

claim: Polymerase stimulates the helicase by increasing the unwinding rate-constant (kcat).
source: The synergistic shift in equilibrium of junction base pair melting by combined enzymes explains the cooperativity, wherein helicase stimulates the polymerase by promoting dNTP binding (decreasing dNTP Km), polymerase stimulates the helicase by increasing the unwinding rate-constant (kcat), consequently the combined enzymes unwind DNA with kinetic parameters resembling enzymes translocating on single-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is shown by kinetic data where helicase kcat increases from ~20 bp/s to ~150 bp/s in the presence of DNAP (Figure 3F).

claim: The combined enzymes unwind DNA with kinetic parameters resembling enzymes translocating on single-stranded DNA.
source: The synergistic shift in equilibrium of junction base pair melting by combined enzymes explains the cooperativity, wherein helicase stimulates the polymerase by promoting dNTP binding (decreasing dNTP Km), polymerase stimulates the helicase by increasing the unwinding rate-constant (kcat), consequently the combined enzymes unwind DNA with kinetic parameters resembling enzymes translocating on single-stranded DNA.
evidence: The kinetic parameters of combined enzymes (kcat ~90 bp/s, Km ~90-120 μM) are similar to those on ssDNA substrates.

claim: Replicative helicases and DNA polymerases are not efficient at unwinding duplex DNA when working independently.
source: Replicative helicases and DNA polymerases (DNAPs) are not efficient at unwinding the duplex DNA when they are working independently.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Kim et al., 1996; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2001; Galletto et al., 2004; Stano et al., 2005; Lionnet et al., 2007; Donmez and Patel, 2008).

claim: The unwinding rates of isolated helicases and polymerases are slower than their translocation rates on single-stranded DNA.
source: The unwinding rates are slower than their translocation rates on single-stranded (ss) DNA and slower than the rates of DNA replication (Kim et al., 1996; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2001; Galletto et al., 2004; Stano et al., 2005; Lionnet et al., 2007; Donmez and Patel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The unwinding rates of isolated helicases decrease steeply with increasing GC percentage in the duplex DNA.
source: Moreover, the unwinding rates of isolated helicases decrease steeply with increasing GC percentage in the duplex DNA, therefore, assisting forces that destabilize the junction base pairs stimulate the helicase (Galletto et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2007; Lionnet et al., 2007; Donmez and Patel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 2D showing helicase kcat decreases from 65 to 15 bp/s with increasing GC content.

claim: In the presence of an actively synthesizing replicative DNAP, the unwinding rates of the helicase become fast and GC independent.
source: However, in the presence of an actively synthesizing replicative DNAP, the unwinding rates of the helicase become fast and GC independent (Kim et al., 1996; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2001; Stano et al., 2005; Manosas et al., 2012b; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 3B-D showing minimal GC dependence for combined enzymes.

claim: Replicative DNAPs on their own have limited strand displacement synthesis activity, restricted to 4–6 base pairs in T7 DNAP.
source: Similarly, replicative DNAPs on their own have limited strand displacement synthesis activity, restricted to 4–6 base pairs in T7 DNAP (Stano et al., 2005; Yuan and McHenry, 2009; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Isolated DNAPs often stall and move backward to excise the nascent DNA using their proofreading exonuclease activity when faced with downstream duplex DNA.
source: The isolated DNAPs often stall and move backward to excise the nascent DNA using their proofreading exonuclease activity when faced with downstream duplex DNA (Manosas et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of helicase or single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) inhibits processive excision of the nascent DNA and allows DNAP to catalyze fast and processive strand displacement synthesis.
source: The presence of helicase or single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) inhibits processive excision of the nascent DNA and allows DNAP to catalyze fast and processive strand displacement synthesis (Manosas et al., 2012b; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data showing T7 DNAP fully unwinds fork DNA with E. coli SSB (Figure 1B).

claim: Functional coupling between helicase and DNAP was originally identified in prokaryotic systems (T7, T4 bacteriophage, Escherichia coli).
source: Originally identified in prokaryotic systems (T7, T4 bacteriophage, Escherichia coli), this functional coupling between the helicase and DNAP is found also in eukaryotic replication systems (Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the history of discovery in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Functional coupling between helicase and DNAP is found in eukaryotic replication systems.
source: Originally identified in prokaryotic systems (T7, T4 bacteriophage, Escherichia coli), this functional coupling between the helicase and DNAP is found also in eukaryotic replication systems (Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: T7 and E. coli DNAPs are capable of strand displacement synthesis in the presence of SSB with rates comparable to their replication rates.
source: For example, T7 and E. coli DNAPs are capable of strand displacement synthesis in the presence of SSB with rates comparable to their replication rates (Yuan and McHenry, 2009; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data showing T7 DNAP unwinding kcat of 140-190 bp/s with SSB (Figure 1D).

claim: T7 helicase and T7 DNAP exhibit highly coordinated catalysis, whereby helicase hydrolyzes one dNTP for every dNMP incorporated by the DNAP.
source: As combined enzymes, T7 helicase and T7 DNAP exhibit highly coordinated catalysis, whereby helicase hydrolyzes one dNTP for every dNMP incorporated by the DNAP (Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Exonuclease mapping showed that T7 DNAP is located with the T7 helicase in close proximity to the fork junction.
source: Exonuclease mapping showed that T7 DNAP is located with the T7 helicase in close proximity to the fork junction and in a position to influence the junction base pairs (Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There are no structures of replisomes with the exception of a small angle X-Ray scattering structure of the T7 helicase-T7 DNAP bound to ssDNA and primer template DNA.
source: Similarly, there are no structures of replisomes with the exception of a small angle X-Ray scattering structure of the T7 helicase-T7 DNAP bound to ssDNA and primer template DNA, respectively (Kulczyk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of structural knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The low-resolution structure in the absence of a replication fork DNA does not provide the location of the DNAP and helicase at the replication fork junction.
source: However, the low-resolution structure in the absence of a replication fork DNA does not provide the location of the DNAP and helicase at the replication fork junction to understand which enzyme is involved in melting the base pair at the fork junction.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the existing structural data.

claim: T7 DNAP on its own does not unwind the 40 bp replication fork at fast rates.
source: We find that T7 DNAP on its own does not unwind the 40 bp replication fork at fast rates, which is consistent with our previously reported gel-based studies showing T7 DNAP stalling after 4–6 base pairs synthesis (Stano et al., 2005; Pandey and Patel, 2014) and this can be overcome by adding SSB (Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous work.

claim: T7 DNAP fully unwinds the fork DNA with E. coli SSB in the reactions.
source: Indeed, T7 DNAP fully unwinds the fork DNA with E. coli SSB in the reactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence-based unwinding assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: E. coli SSB can be replaced with T7 gp2.5 for stimulating T7 DNAP unwinding activity.
source: Note that we can replace E. coli SSB with T7 gp2.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Myers and Romano, 1988; Nakai and Richardson, 1988; Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: E. coli SSB has higher affinity for ssDNA (0.1–10 nM) than T7 gp2.5.
source: However, we have used E. coli SSB because of its higher affinity for ssDNA (0.1–10 nM) (Molineux et al., 1975), requiring lower amounts of SSB for the same degree of stimulation as with T7 gp2.5 (200 nM SSB vs 3 μM T7 gp2.5) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation and experimental data comparing SSB and gp2.5 concentrations.

claim: E. coli SSB does not unwind DNA on its own.
source: The E. coli SSB does not unwind DNA on its own (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The unwinding rates of T7 DNAP (with SSB) increase in a hyperbolic manner with increasing dNTPs concentrations.
source: The unwinding rates of T7 DNAP (with SSB) increase in a hyperbolic manner with increasing dNTPs concentrations with each of the GC forks (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: At low-dNTPs concentration, the unwinding rates of T7 DNAP are GC-sensitive.
source: At low-dNTPs concentration, the unwinding rates are GC-sensitive, but the rates reach a similarly high value at saturating dNTPs concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1C where rates differ at low dNTP concentrations for different GC content substrates.

claim: The unwinding kcat of T7 DNAP remains nearly constant and ranges from 190 to 140 bp/s as GC percentage increases.
source: Thus, the unwinding kcat remains nearly constant and ranges from 190 to 140 bp/s as GC percentage increases (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1D.

claim: The dNTPs Km of T7 DNAP increases steeply from 40 μM to 270 μM as the GC percentage increases.
source: However, the dNTPs Km increases steeply from 40 μM to 270 μM as the GC percentage increases (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1E.

claim: DNA unwinding-synthesis by T7 DNAP (with SSB) is rate-limited by base pair separation at low-dNTPs concentrations, but not at high dNTPs.
source: This indicates that DNA unwinding-synthesis by T7 DNAP (with SSB) is rate-limited by base pair separation at low-dNTPs concentrations, but not at high dNTPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the GC-dependent Km and GC-independent kcat data.

claim: When the downstream DNA is single-stranded, the dNTPs Km is 10–20 μM and the rate of synthesis is ∼200 nt/s.
source: For comparison, when the downstream DNA is single-stranded and does not need to be melted, the dNTPs Km is 10–20 μM and the rate of synthesis is ∼200 nt/s (Patel et al., 1991; Stano et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The dNTPs Km on duplex DNA template is 2–10 times higher than on ssDNA template.
source: Thus, the dNTPs Km on duplex DNA template is 2–10 times higher than on ssDNA template.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the Km values on duplex DNA (40-270 μM) to ssDNA (10-20 μM).

claim: The equilibrium constant for the base-capture step (K1) decreases steadily with increasing GC percentage.
source: The rate vs dNTPs dependencies of all GC forks fit well to this ordered three-step mechanism (Appendix—Section 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) with variable equilibrium constant for the base-capture step (K1), which we find decreases steadily with increasing GC percentage (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1G obtained from kinetic modeling.

claim: The downstream DNA stability mainly affects the base-capture step of T7 DNAP.
source: This means that the downstream DNA stability mainly affects the base-capture step, and DNAP is less efficient at capturing the templating-base when the stability of the duplex DNA is higher.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic modeling showing K1 decreases with increasing GC content.

claim: dNTP binding stabilizes the base-captured state and drives DNA unwinding by T7 DNAP.
source: However, the nearly GC-independent DNA unwinding kcat indicates that dNTP binding stabilizes the base-captured state and drives DNA unwinding, but higher concentrations of dNTPs are required with higher GC percentage in the downstream DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing GC-independent kcat but GC-dependent Km.

claim: The mechanism of T7 DNAP resembles the mechanism proposed for DNA-dependent RNA polymerases.
source: This mechanism of DNAP resembles the mechanism proposed for DNA-dependent RNA polymerases (Thomen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by citation.

claim: The unwinding kcat of T7 helicase decreases from 65 bp/s to 15 bp/s with increasing GC percentage.
source: Unlike T7 DNAP, the unwinding kcat of the helicase decreases from 65 bp/s to 15 bp/s with increasing GC percentage (Figure 2D), but the dTTP Km remains relatively unchanged and decreases only two-fold from 300 μM to 160 μM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2D.

claim: The dTTP Km of T7 helicase remains relatively unchanged and decreases only two-fold from 300 μM to 160 μM with increasing GC percentage.
source: Unlike T7 DNAP, the unwinding kcat of the helicase decreases from 65 bp/s to 15 bp/s with increasing GC percentage (Figure 2D), but the dTTP Km remains relatively unchanged and decreases only two-fold from 300 μM to 160 μM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2E.

claim: T7 helicase and T7 DNAP respond differently to increasing GC content, indicating their DNA-unwinding mechanisms are fundamentally different.
source: Thus, T7 helicase and T7 DNAP respond differently to increasing GC content, which indicates that their DNA-unwinding mechanisms are fundamentally different.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the kinetic responses to GC content for helicase (kcat decreases, Km constant) vs DNAP (kcat constant, Km increases).

claim: T7 helicase moves on DNA through sequential nucleotide hydrolysis and translocation mechanism.
source: T7 helicase moves on DNA through sequential nucleotide hydrolysis and translocation mechanism, where each subunit of the ring takes turn in binding the incoming nucleotide (Liao et al., 2005; Crampton et al., 2006; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Thomsen and Berger, 2009; Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At any given time, only the leading subunit of T7 helicase binds an incoming dTTP and reels in the nucleotide base from the fork junction.
source: Therefore at any given time, only the leading subunit of T7 helicase binds an incoming dTTP and reels in the nucleotide base from the fork junction (Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The kinetic data for T7 helicase fit well to the random order mechanism where base-capture can occur both in the dTTP-free and dTTP-bound states.
source: Therefore, we considered all three models and our kinetic modeling shows that the rate vs dTTP data do not fit to models where dTTP binding and base-capture steps occur in a particular order (Appendix—Section 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C). Instead, the data fit well to the random order mechanism (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), wherein base-capture can occur both in the dTTP-free and dTTP-bound states of the leading subunit.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic modeling shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dTTP-bound state of T7 helicase is slightly better at capturing the DNA-base than the dTTP-free state.
source: We show that the dTTP-bound state is slightly better at capturing the DNA-base than the dTTP-free state (Figure 2H), but the equilibrium constants of the base-capture steps in the dTTP-free (K1) and dTTP-bound (K2) states both decrease with increasing GC percentage (Figure 2G–H), which indicates that the rate of unwinding by the helicase is limited by base pair separation even at high concentrations of dTTP.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The equilibrium constants of the base-capture steps in the dTTP-free (K1) and dTTP-bound (K2) states both decrease with increasing GC percentage.
source: We show that the dTTP-bound state is slightly better at capturing the DNA-base than the dTTP-free state (Figure 2H), but the equilibrium constants of the base-capture steps in the dTTP-free (K1) and dTTP-bound (K2) states both decrease with increasing GC percentage (Figure 2G–H), which indicates that the rate of unwinding by the helicase is limited by base pair separation even at high concentrations of dTTP.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The rate of unwinding by T7 helicase is limited by base pair separation even at high concentrations of dTTP.
source: We show that the dTTP-bound state is slightly better at capturing the DNA-base than the dTTP-free state (Figure 2H), but the equilibrium constants of the base-capture steps in the dTTP-free (K1) and dTTP-bound (K2) states both decrease with increasing GC percentage (Figure 2G–H), which indicates that the rate of unwinding by the helicase is limited by base pair separation even at high concentrations of dTTP.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic modeling showing K1 and K2 decrease with GC content.

claim: T7 DNAP follows an ordered mechanism, wherein dNTP binding follows the base-capture step.
source: T7 DNAP follows an ordered mechanism, wherein dNTP binding follows the base-capture step.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic modeling shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The kinetic outcome of increasing GC content on T7 DNAP is analogous to a pure competitive mechanism where inhibitor (GC content) increases the dNTPs Km without affecting the unwinding kcat.
source: Therefore, the kinetic outcome of increasing GC content is analogous to a pure competitive mechanism where inhibitor (GC content) increases the dNTPs Km without affecting the unwinding kcat.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing GC-dependent Km but GC-independent kcat.

claim: T7 helicase does not follow an ordered mechanism.
source: T7 helicase does not follow an ordered mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic modeling showing the random order mechanism fits best (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The kinetic outcome of increasing GC content on T7 helicase is analogous to a mixed inhibition mechanism where inhibitor (GC content) decreases the unwinding kcat and mildly affects the dTTP Km.
source: Consequently, the kinetic outcome of increasing GC content is analogous to a mixed inhibition mechanism where inhibitor (GC content) decreases the unwinding kcat and mildly affects the dTTP Km.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing GC-dependent kcat and mildly GC-dependent Km.

claim: T7 DNAP is able to achieve fast rates of unwinding at high dNTPs.
source: Therefore, T7 DNAP is able to achieve fast rates of unwinding at high dNTPs, but this is not the case with the helicase, whose unwinding kcat remains suboptimal even at high-dTTP concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1C-D where DNAP reaches high rates at saturating dNTP concentrations.

claim: T7 helicase's unwinding kcat remains suboptimal even at high-dTTP concentrations.
source: Therefore, T7 DNAP is able to achieve fast rates of unwinding at high dNTPs, but this is not the case with the helicase, whose unwinding kcat remains suboptimal even at high-dTTP concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 2C-D where helicase kcat remains low even at high dTTP concentrations.

claim: The unwinding kcat of combined T7 helicase and T7 DNAP is ∼90 bp/s when GC percentage is low, and decreases minimally to 70 bp/s when GC percentage is high.
source: The unwinding kcat is ∼90 bp/s when GC percentage is low, and kcat decreases minimally to 70 bp/s when GC percentage is high.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3C.

claim: The dTTP Km of combined enzymes changes little from 120 to 90 μM as GC percentage increases.
source: Similarly, the dTTP Km changes little from 120 to 90 μM as GC percentage increases (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3D.

claim: The DNA-unwinding rates of the combined enzymes are not rate-limited by base pair separation at any dNTPs concentrations.
source: This indicates that the DNA-unwinding rates of the combined enzymes are not rate-limited by base pair separation at any dNTPs concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the minimal GC dependence of both kcat and Km for combined enzymes.

claim: The two enzymes mutually stimulate the activities of unwinding and synthesis.
source: Additionally, these results also show that the two enzymes mutually stimulate the activities of unwinding and synthesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the kinetic parameters of isolated vs combined enzymes (Figures 1-3).

claim: The dTTP Km of the isolated helicase on the 50% GC fork is ∼160 μM, which decreases to ∼80 μM in the presence of T7 DNAP.
source: The dTTP Km of the isolated helicase on the 50% GC fork is ∼160 μM, which decreases to ∼80 μM in the presence of T7 DNAP (Figure 3E), which is close to the dTTP Km on ssDNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3E.

claim: The unwinding kcat of the isolated helicase is ∼20 bp/s and increases substantially to ∼150 bp/s in the presence of T7 DNAP.
source: Similarly, the unwinding kcat of the isolated helicase is ∼20 bp/s and increases substantially to ∼150 bp/s in the presence of T7 DNAP (Figure 3F), which is close to the translocation rate of the helicase on ssDNA (∼130 nt/s) (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3F.

claim: T7 DNAP stimulates T7 helicase by increasing the DNA-unwinding kcat and by slightly decreasing the dTTP Km.
source: Thus, T7 DNAP stimulates T7 helicase by increasing the DNA-unwinding kcat and by slightly decreasing the dTTP Km.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing kinetic parameters of isolated helicase vs helicase with DNAP (Figure 3E-F).

claim: The kinetic parameters of T7 helicase coupled to T7 DNAP resemble those of helicase translocating on ssDNA rather than unwinding duplex DNA.
source: The kinetic parameters of T7 helicase coupled to T7 DNAP resemble those of helicase translocating on ssDNA rather than unwinding duplex DNA.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the kinetic parameters of helicase-DNAP to those on ssDNA substrates.

claim: The unwinding kcat of T7 DNAP (with SSB) is 160 bp/s and decreases minimally to 140 bp/s in the presence of T7 helicase.
source: The unwinding kcat (with SSB) is 160 bp/s and decreases minimally to 140 bp/s in the presence of T7 helicase, whereas the dNTPs Km decreases by 24-fold from ∼120 μM (with SSB) to 5 µM in the presence of T7 helicase (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3G.

claim: The dNTPs Km of T7 DNAP decreases by 24-fold from ∼120 μM (with SSB) to 5 µM in the presence of T7 helicase.
source: The unwinding kcat (with SSB) is 160 bp/s and decreases minimally to 140 bp/s in the presence of T7 helicase, whereas the dNTPs Km decreases by 24-fold from ∼120 μM (with SSB) to 5 µM in the presence of T7 helicase (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3G.

claim: The 5 μM dNTPs Km is slightly lower than the DNAP's dNTP Km on ssDNA template (∼10–20 μM).
source: The 5 μM dNTPs Km is slightly lower than the DNAP's dNTP Km on ssDNA template (∼10–20 μM) (Patel et al., 1991; Stano et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison to values from previous work supported by citations.

claim: T7 helicase stimulates T7 DNAP by promoting dNTP binding.
source: Thus, T7 helicase stimulates T7 DNAP by promoting dNTP binding, and in the presence of helicase, T7 DNAP behaves like a motor translocating on ssDNA template.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the large decrease in dNTP Km when helicase is present (Figure 3G).

claim: In the presence of helicase, T7 DNAP behaves like a motor translocating on ssDNA template.
source: Thus, T7 helicase stimulates T7 DNAP by promoting dNTP binding, and in the presence of helicase, T7 DNAP behaves like a motor translocating on ssDNA template.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic parameters of DNAP with helicase resembling those on ssDNA.

claim: The lower kcat of the helicase and higher dNTPs Km of DNAP when functioning independently are due to inefficient capture of the nucleotide base from the fork junction.
source: When functioning independently, the lower kcat of the helicase and higher dNTPs Km of DNAP are due to inefficient capture of the nucleotide base from the fork junction.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic modeling showing base-capture equilibrium constants decrease with GC content.

claim: The two enzymes help each other by increasing the efficiency of the base-capture step.
source: This implies that the two enzymes help each other by increasing the efficiency of the base-capture step.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual stimulation effects and the kinetic modeling results.

claim: When helicase rate is decreased by lowering dTTP, DNA unwinding slows down.
source: When the helicase rate is decreased by lowering dTTP, DNA unwinding slows down (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4A.

claim: At 500 μM dTTP, the kcat of the combined enzymes is fast (150 bp/s), but at 50 μM dTTP, the kcat is 60 bp/s.
source: At 500 μM dTTP, the kcat of the combined enzymes is fast (150 bp/s), but at 50 μM dTTP, the kcat is 60 bp/s.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4A.

claim: When helicase is slower than DNAP, the DNAP will not outrun the helicase.
source: This implies that when helicase is slower than DNAP, the DNAP will not outrun the helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unwinding rate decreases when helicase is slowed down.

claim: The dVTPs Km of the combined enzymes remains unchanged at ∼5 μM, both at low- and high-dTTP concentrations.
source: Interestingly, the dVTPs Km of the combined enzymes remains unchanged at ∼5 μM, both at low- and high-dTTP concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4A.

claim: When helicase is slower than DNAP, the combined enzymes remain functionally coupled.
source: This means that when helicase is slower than DNAP, the combined enzymes remain functionally coupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged dVTP Km at different dTTP concentrations.

claim: When DNAP cannot move forward due to lack of dNTPs, the associated helicase unwinds the replication fork with unstimulated rates.
source: When DNAP cannot move forward due to lack of dNTPs, the associated helicase unwinds the replication fork with unstimulated rates (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4B.

claim: The stalled DNAP does not pull the helicase back or prevent it from unwinding the DNA.
source: This means that the stalled DNAP does not pull the helicase back or prevent it from unwinding the DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that helicase unwinds at its normal rate when DNAP is stalled.

claim: With stalled DNAP, the unwinding rate of the 50% GC fork is 20 bp/s, which is similar to the rate of helicase functioning independently (18 bp/s).
source: With stalled DNAP, the unwinding rate of the 50% GC fork is 20 bp/s, which is similar to the rate of helicase functioning independently (18 bp/s).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4B.

claim: With the stalled DNAP, the dTTP Km of the helicase is ~130 μM, which is similar to the dTTP Km in the absence of DNAP (~160 μM).
source: Similarly, with the stalled DNAP, the dTTP Km of the helicase is ~130 μM, which is similar to the dTTP Km in the absence of DNAP (~160 μM) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4B.

claim: Stalling the DNAP functionally uncouples the helicase.
source: Thus, stalling the DNAP functionally uncouples the helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that helicase kinetic parameters revert to those of isolated helicase when DNAP is stalled.

claim: When dVTPs concentrations are low (0.5 μM), the unwinding rate with the combined enzymes is similar to that of the isolated helicase.
source: When dVTPs concentrations are low (0.5 μM), the unwinding rate with the combined enzymes is similar to that of the isolated helicase (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4C.

claim: When T7 DNAP is slow, the helicase is capable of moving faster and can outrun the DNAP.
source: This indicates that when T7 DNAP is slow, the helicase is capable of moving faster and can outrun the DNAP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unwinding rate matches helicase rate when DNAP is slow.

claim: When 2-AP is base-paired, it has a low-fluorescence intensity, but when 2-AP:T base pair is melted and the 2-AP base is unstacked, the fluorescence increases.
source: When 2-AP is base-paired (Figure 5A), it has a low-fluorescence intensity, but when 2-AP:T base pair is melted and the 2-AP base is unstacked, the fluorescence increases (Ward et al., 1969).
evidence: This is a well-established property of 2-AP supported by citation.

claim: Changes in 2-AP fluorescence successfully monitor base unstacking and base pair separation in a variety of enzyme studies, including replication enzymes.
source: Such changes in 2-AP fluorescence successfully monitor base unstacking and base pair separation in a variety of enzyme studies, including replication enzymes (Reha-Krantz, 2009; Jose et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The crystal structure of T7 DNAP shows interactions with two template-bases (N + 1 and N + 2) immediately downstream of the primer-end at position N.
source: The crystal structure of T7 DNAP (Doublie et al., 1998) shows interactions with two template-bases (N + 1 and N + 2) immediately downstream of the primer-end at positon N and ∼90o bend between N + 1 and N + 2 template-bases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The crystal structure of T7 DNAP shows ∼90° bend between N + 1 and N + 2 template-bases.
source: The crystal structure of T7 DNAP (Doublie et al., 1998) shows interactions with two template-bases (N + 1 and N + 2) immediately downstream of the primer-end at positon N and ∼90o bend between N + 1 and N + 2 template-bases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Introducing a 2-AP at N + 1 results in a significant increase in fluorescence consistent with unstacking of the N + 1 base from bending of the template DNA.
source: Thus, introducing a 2-AP at N + 1 results in a significant increase in fluorescence consistent with unstacking of the N + 1 base from bending of the template DNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5D.

claim: There is no increase in fluorescence of 2-AP at N + 2 and a decrease is observed at N + 3 upon T7 DNAP binding.
source: However, there is no increase in fluorescence of 2-AP at N + 2 and a decrease is observed at N + 3 (Figure 5D), which is consistent with interactions of these template DNA-bases with the amino acids in the template-binding pocket of T7 DNAP (Doublie et al., 1998).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5D.

claim: The change in 2-AP fluorescence at positions N + 4 and N + 5 is minimal upon DNAP binding, indicating that T7 DNAP may not interact with these downstream positions.
source: The change in 2-AP fluorescence at positions N + 4 and N + 5 is minimal upon DNAP binding, which indicates that T7 DNAP may not interact with these downstream positions.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5D.

claim: T7 DNAP influences only three template-bases immediately downstream from the primer-end.
source: Thus, T7 DNAP influences only three template-bases immediately downstream from the primer-end.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP fluorescence data showing changes only at N+1, N+2, and N+3 positions.

claim: The fluorescence intensity increases upon adding T7 DNAP when 2-AP is at the N + 1, N + 2, or N + 3 base pair in the lagging strand, but not at N + 4.
source: The fluorescence intensity increases upon adding T7 DNAP when 2-AP is at the N + 1, N + 2, or N + 3 base pair, but not at N + 4 (Figure 5E–H—Green bars).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5E-H.

claim: T7 DNAP does not melt the junction base pair three nucleotides downstream from the primer-end.
source: However, when 2-AP is at N + 3 and is part of the fork junction, no increase in fluorescence is observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), which indicates that T7 DNAP does not melt the junction base pair three nucleotides downstream from the primer-end.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The increase in 2-AP intensity at N + 3 in the internal position is due to N + 2 base unstacking and not from unstacking of the N + 3 base.
source: The increase in 2-AP intensity at N + 3 in the internal position (Figure 5G) is due to N + 2 base unstacking and not from unstacking of the N + 3 base.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing results with 2-AP at N+3 in internal vs junction positions.

claim: T7 DNAP binds to three template-bases downstream of primer-end and melts two base pairs.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that T7 DNAP binds to three template-bases downstream of primer-end and melts two base pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP fluorescence data at various positions.

claim: When 2-AP experiments with T7 DNAP were carried out with E. coli SSB, the fluorescence intensity changes were much larger.
source: When 2-AP experiments with T7 DNAP were carried out with E. coli SSB, the fluorescence intensity changes were much larger, although SSB by itself did not increase the 2-AP fluorescence significantly (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: T7 DNAP on its own only partially melts the junction base pairs.
source: These results indicate that T7 DNAP on its own only partially melts the junction base pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SSB greatly enhances the fluorescence increase caused by DNAP.

claim: The junction base pairs appear to be in dynamic equilibrium (closed ↔ open) when T7 DNAP is bound.
source: Furthermore, these base pairs appear to be in dynamic equilibrium (closed ↔ open), because SSB can shift the equilibrium towards the open state by simply binding to ssDNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SSB enhances melting without directly interacting with duplex DNA.

claim: T7 DNAP can melt the junction base pair, but DNAP is not efficient at preventing base pair reannealing.
source: This provides direct proof that T7 DNAP can melt the junction base pair, but DNAP is not efficient at preventing base pair reannealing; thus, SSB stimulates the activity of DNAP by trapping the unwound bases.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP data showing partial melting by DNAP alone and enhanced melting with SSB.

claim: SSB stimulates the activity of DNAP by trapping the unwound bases.
source: This provides direct proof that T7 DNAP can melt the junction base pair, but DNAP is not efficient at preventing base pair reannealing; thus, SSB stimulates the activity of DNAP by trapping the unwound bases.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP data showing SSB enhances melting by DNAP.

claim: T7 helicase increases the fluorescence of 2-AP at the fork junction, but not the second base pair from the junction.
source: However, T7 helicase increases the fluorescence of 2-AP at the fork junction, but not the second base pair from the junction, irrespective of the gap size between the primer end and fork junction (Figure 5E–H—Red bars).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Unlike T7 DNAP that melts two base pairs upon binding to the replication fork substrate, T7 helicase melts only the junction base pair.
source: Thus, unlike T7 DNAP that melts two base pairs upon binding to the replication fork substrate, T7 helicase melts only the junction base pair.
evidence: This is shown by comparing 2-AP data for helicase vs DNAP in Figure 5E-H.

claim: T7 helicase melts the junction base pair even when the primer-end is separated from the fork junction by more than one nucleotide.
source: However, T7 helicase melts the junction base pair even when the primer-end is separated from the fork junction by more than one nucleotide (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C compare to Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: T7 helicase follows the fork junction and is not influenced by the position of the primer-end.
source: These results indicate that T7 helicase follows the fork junction and is not influenced by the position of the primer-end.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that helicase melts the junction base pair regardless of gap size.

claim: SSB has no effect on the helicase catalyzed melting of the fork junction.
source: Interestingly, SSB has no effect on the helicase catalyzed melting of the fork junction (Figure 5—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5D.

claim: SSB does not stimulate the unwinding rates of the helicase.
source: This is consistent with the observation that SSB does not stimulate the unwinding rates of the helicase (Donmez and Patel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The combined enzymes show a much larger increase in fluorescence intensity with 2-AP at N + 1, N + 2, or N + 3 base pairs, but not at N + 4.
source: The combined enzymes show a much larger increase in fluorescence intensity with 2-AP at N + 1, N + 2, or N + 3 base pairs, but not at N + 4.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5E-H (light blue bars).

claim: The combined enzymes melt two base pairs downstream from the primer-end, just like T7 DNAP, but more efficiently.
source: As shown earlier with the DNAP, the increase in N + 3 is due to N + 2 base unstacking; therefore, the results indicate that the combined enzymes melt two base pairs downstream from the primer-end, just like T7 DNAP, but more efficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP data comparing combined enzymes to isolated DNAP.

claim: The small increase in fluorescence intensity with the isolated helicase and DNAP suggests that each enzyme shifts the equilibrium only moderately to the base-pair melted state.
source: The small increase in fluorescence intensity with the isolated helicase and DNAP suggests that each enzyme shifts the equilibrium only moderately to the base-pair melted state.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP fluorescence data showing modest increases with isolated enzymes.

claim: The striking increase in fluorescence intensity with the combined enzymes indicates that together the two enzymes shift the equilibrium strongly toward the base-pair melted state.
source: On the other hand, the striking increase in fluorescence intensity with the combined enzymes indicates that together the two enzymes shift the equilibrium strongly toward the base-pair melted state.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP fluorescence data showing large increases with combined enzymes.

claim: The combined effect of helicase and DNAP on base pairs melting is greater than the sum, which indicates synergism in DNA melting.
source: Interestingly, the combined effect of helicase and DNAP on base pairs melting is greater than the sum, which indicates synergism in DNA melting.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the fluorescence increases with isolated vs combined enzymes.

claim: Synergistic melting of the base pair is observed only when there is no gap or one nucleotide gap between the primer-end and fork junction.
source: This synergism depends on the number of nucleotides between the primer-end and fork junction. Synergistic melting of the base pair is observed only when there is no gap or one nucleotide gap between the primer-end (DNAP-binding site) and fork junction (helicase-binding site) (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Synergistic melting is not observed when there are two nucleotides between the primer-end and fork junction.
source: Synergistic melting is not observed when there are two nucleotides between the primer-end and fork junction (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5H.

claim: A replication fork with two ssDNA template-bases between the primer-end and fork junction can stably accommodate both enzymes of the T7 replisome.
source: The results also demonstrate that a replication fork with two ssDNA template-bases between the primer-end and fork junction can stably accommodate both enzymes of the T7 replisome.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP data showing both enzymes can bind and function with appropriate spacing.

claim: T7 DNAP by itself melts two base pairs upon binding to the replication fork DNA.
source: In fact, T7 DNAP by itself melts two base pairs upon binding to the replication fork DNA. This was unexpected, because DNA synthesis occurs in steps of one nucleotide, which would require unwinding of only one base pair at a time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2-AP fluorescence data in Figure 5E-G.

claim: T7 DNAP destabilizes two base pairs of duplex DNA upon initial binding to the forked DNA to create two ss nucleotides for its template-binding pocket.
source: Based on our 2-AP studies here and the crystal structure of T7 DNAP (Doublie et al., 1998), we propose that T7 DNAP destabilizes two base pairs of duplex DNA upon initial binding to the forked DNA to create two ss nucleotides for its template-binding pocket.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on 2-AP data and crystal structure.

claim: Two or more template-bases in the downstream template-binding pocket have been observed in crystal structures of other DNAPs as well.
source: Two or more template-bases in the downstream template-binding pocket have been observed in crystal structures of other DNAPs as well (Doublie et al., 1998; Johnson et al., 2003; Berman et al., 2007; Jain et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures of other polymerases.

claim: This mode of DNA binding could be a general feature of replicative DNAPs.
source: Hence, this mode of DNA binding could be a general feature of replicative DNAPs.
evidence: This is speculated based on observations in multiple polymerase structures.

claim: T7 helicase on its own can melt the junction base pair, but it melts only one base pair and follows the fork junction.
source: We show that T7 helicase on its own can also melt the junction base pair, but it melts only one base pair and follows the fork junction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2-AP fluorescence data in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The junction base pair is melted only partially by the isolated enzymes.
source: Comparing DNA melting by isolated and combined enzymes reveals that the junction base pair is melted only partially by the isolated enzymes (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is shown by the 2-AP fluorescence data in Figure 5E-H.

claim: The partial melting of junction base pairs by isolated enzymes explains the slow and GC sensitive unwinding rates of the isolated enzymes.
source: This explains the slow and GC sensitive unwinding rates of the isolated enzymes in our kinetic experiments (Figures 1C, 2C).
evidence: This is inferred by connecting the 2-AP melting data to the kinetic data.

claim: The junction base pair is melted more efficiently by the combined enzymes, explaining fast and GC-independent rates of the combined enzymes.
source: The junction base pair is melted more efficiently by the combined enzymes, explaining fast and GC-independent rates of the combined enzymes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred by connecting the 2-AP melting data to the kinetic data.

claim: The combined enzymes melted two base pairs upon binding to the fork DNA initially to establish the catalytically competent structure of the replication fork.
source: We observed that the combined enzymes melted two base pairs upon binding to the fork DNA. We propose that this occurs initially to establish the catalytically competent structure of the replication fork—T7 DNAP melts two base pairs and binds two ssDNA nucleotides in its template-binding pocket, which positions the helicase two nucleotides ahead at the fork junction, as shown in Figure 6.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the 2-AP data and structural considerations.

claim: During active leading strand synthesis, the enzymes melt only one base pair at the fork junction at a time consistent with the one nucleotide chemical step size of the combined enzymes.
source: We propose that during active leading strand synthesis, the enzymes melt only one base pair at the fork junction at a time consistent with the one nucleotide chemical step size of the combined enzymes (Pandey and Patel, 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the step size data from previous work.

claim: The DNAP by itself is not efficient at preventing junction base pair reannealing, and this unfavorable equilibrium constant for DNA melting destabilizes the post-translocated state of DNAP and competes with incoming dNTP binding.
source: Based on our results, we propose that the DNAP by itself is not efficient at preventing junction base pair reannealing, and this unfavorable equilibrium constant for DNA melting destabilizes the post-translocated state of DNAP and competes with incoming dNTP binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the 2-AP and kinetic data.

claim: When helicase is present at the fork junction, it helps both unwind and trap the junction bases.
source: When helicase is present at the fork junction, it helps both unwind and trap the junction bases.
evidence: This is inferred from the synergistic melting observed with combined enzymes.

claim: The associated helicase stimulates dNTP binding by stabilizing the post-translocated state of T7 DNAP, and the outcome is decrease in dNTPs Km.
source: Thus, the associated helicase stimulates dNTP binding by stabilizing the post-translocated state of T7 DNAP, and the outcome is decrease in dNTPs Km.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the kinetic data showing decreased Km with helicase.

claim: The associated DNAP by providing an unwound base to the helicase at the fork junction facilitates the base-capture step and drives the reactions of dTTP binding-hydrolysis-product release around the helicase ring, and the outcome is an increase in the unwinding kcat.
source: The associated DNAP by providing an unwound base to the helicase at the fork junction facilitates the base-capture step and drives the reactions of dTTP binding-hydrolysis-product release around the helicase ring, and the outcome is an increase in the unwinding kcat.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the kinetic data showing increased kcat with DNAP.

claim: The combined binding energy of the two enzymes bound to opposite strands is sufficient to keep the unwound bases from reannealing, explaining the fast and GC-independent unwinding rates of helicase-DNAP.
source: The combined binding energy of the two enzymes bound to opposite strands is sufficient to keep the unwound bases from reannealing, explaining the fast and GC-independent unwinding rates of helicase-DNAP.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the synergistic melting and kinetic data.

claim: Cooperative and enhanced efficiency of base pair melting is observed only when the helicase and DNAP are within one nucleotide distance from each other.
source: Interestingly, cooperative and enhanced efficiency of base pair melting is observed only when the helicase and DNAP are within one nucleotide distance from each other.
evidence: This is shown by the 2-AP data in Figure 5E-H showing synergism only with 0-1 nucleotide gaps.

claim: In most cases, helicase is coupled physically to the DNAP, either directly as in the case of T7 replication system or indirectly through accessory proteins.
source: In most cases, helicase is coupled physically to the DNAP, either directly as in the case of T7 replication system or indirectly through accessory proteins (Kim et al., 1996; Hamdan et al., 2007; Gambus et al., 2009; Sengupta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some of these interactions aid in the assembly of the replisome and perhaps in proper positioning of the helicase with the DNAP in the replisome.
source: Some of these interactions aid in the assembly of the replisome (Zhang et al., 2011) and perhaps in proper positioning of the helicase with the DNAP in the replisome, but the consequences of breaking physical interactions on synergistic melting need to be investigated.
evidence: This is supported by citation and speculation about the role of physical interactions.

claim: When DNAP stalls or is the slower motor, the helicase becomes functionally uncoupled and outruns the DNAP by unwinding the replication fork at the unstimulated rates.
source: Our investigation of such situations reveals that when DNAP stalls or is the slower motor, the helicase becomes functionally uncoupled and outruns the DNAP by unwinding the replication fork at the unstimulated rates.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Similar behaviors of functional uncoupling when DNAP stalls were observed in other replisome studies as well.
source: Similar behaviors were observed in other replisome studies as well (Byun et al., 2005; McInerney and O'Donnell, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When the helicase slows down, the two enzymes remain functionally coupled as evident from the low dNTPs Km and that the DNAP does not outrun the helicase.
source: Interestingly, when the helicase slows down, the two enzymes remain functionally coupled as evident from the low dNTPs Km and that the DNAP does not outrun the helicase.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4A.

claim: When helicase slows down, the combined enzymes unwind the DNA with the stimulated rate of the helicase.
source: In this case, the combined enzymes unwind the DNA with the stimulated rate of the helicase.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4A.

claim: The unwinding rates of T7 DNAP with SSB remain GC-sensitive at low-dNTPs concentrations.
source: Although SSB stimulates base pair melting by T7 DNAP, our studies find that the unwinding rates of T7 DNAP with SSB remain GC-sensitive at low-dNTPs concentrations.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: SSB cannot trap the junction bases coordinately with DNA synthesis in the manner that T7 helicase does during leading strand synthesis.
source: We propose that this is because SSB cannot trap the junction bases coordinately with DNA synthesis in the manner that T7 helicase does during leading strand synthesis.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the GC-sensitive rates with SSB.

claim: SSB does not increase the unwinding rates of T7 helicase, which remain GC sensitive at all concentrations of dTTP.
source: Similarly, it has been shown previously that SSB does not increase the unwinding rates of T7 helicase, which remain GC sensitive at all concentrations of dTTP (Donmez and Patel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Simply trapping the displaced strand by DNA binding is not sufficient for rate acceleration, but coordination between the steps of junction base pair unwinding/trapping and synthesis is needed.
source: These observations indicate that simply trapping the displaced strand by DNA binding is not sufficient, but coordination between the steps of junction base pair unwinding/trapping and synthesis is needed for rate acceleration.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the effects of SSB vs helicase on unwinding rates.

claim: The replicative helicase is a central player in coordinating leading and lagging strand synthesis.
source: The replicative helicase is a central player in coordinating leading and lagging strand synthesis (Pandey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The interdependency between helicase and DNAP assures that the DNA is not unwound in an uncoupled manner leading to disruption in the coordinated synthesis of the two strands.
source: The interdependency between helicase and DNAP assures that the DNA is not unwound in an uncoupled manner leading to disruption in the coordinated synthesis of the two strands.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional coupling data showing coordination between enzymes.

claim: The mechanism of DNAP is conserved in all organisms where DNAPs elongate the primer in the 3′–5′ direction.
source: The mechanism of DNAP is conserved in all organisms where DNAPs elongate the primer in the 3′–5′ direction.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about polymerase mechanisms.

claim: Replicative helicases of the prokaryotes and phages unwind DNA in the 5′–3′ direction.
source: On the other hand, replicative helicases of the prokaryotes and phages unwind DNA in the 5′–3′ direction, whereas those of eukaryotes unwind DNA in the opposite 3′–5′ direction.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about helicase directionality.

claim: Replicative helicases of eukaryotes unwind DNA in the 3′–5′ direction.
source: On the other hand, replicative helicases of the prokaryotes and phages unwind DNA in the 5′–3′ direction, whereas those of eukaryotes unwind DNA in the opposite 3′–5′ direction.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about helicase directionality.

claim: The leading edges of the T7 helicase and T7 DNAP are close together at the fork junction and this conformation is important for functional coupling of unwinding and synthesis reactions and preventing DNA reannealing.
source: Our studies suggest that the leading edges of the T7 helicase and T7 DNAP are close together at the fork junction and this conformation is important for functional coupling of unwinding and synthesis reactions and preventing DNA reannealing.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2-AP data showing synergism only when enzymes are close together.

claim: This model of the replication fork is likely to be generally applicable to replisomes of prokaryotes as most show functional coupling between helicase and DNAP.
source: This model of the replication fork is likely to be generally applicable to replisomes of prokaryotes as most show functional coupling between helicase and DNAP (Patel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on the general observation of functional coupling in prokaryotes, supported by citation.

claim: In eukaryotic and archaeal replisomes, the replicative helicase binds to the same strand as the DNAP.
source: In contrast to prokaryotic replisomes, the replicative helicase of eukaryotes and archaea binds to the same strand as the DNAP (O'Donnell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In eukaryotic replisomes, both helicase and DNAP cannot be close to the fork junction, and there must be other mechanisms to functionally couple the two activities and prevent junction base pair reannealing.
source: In this case, both helicase and DNAP cannot be close to the fork junction, and there must be other mechanisms to functionally couple the two activities and prevent junction base pair reannealing.
evidence: This is inferred from the different architecture of eukaryotic replisomes.

claim: Although the MCM2-7 helicase encircles the leading strand, other subunits in the CMG (Cdc45-MCM2-7-GINS) complex may interact with the lagging strand and this could be a mechanism for preventing DNA reannealing at the fork junction.
source: It is possible that although the MCM2-7 helicase encircles the leading strand, other subunits in the CMG (Cdc45-MCM2-7-GINS) complex may interact with the lagging strand and this could be a mechanism for preventing DNA reannealing at the fork junction (Costa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about eukaryotic replisome mechanisms, supported by citation.
